lines.text: Your paycheck lands, and three weeks later, you're broke again.
Rent took some. Food took some. A dozen little subscriptions took the rest. And you're left wondering where it all went.
Stop blaming your salary.
It's five moves nobody showed you, and almost none of them cost a cent.
Here's the plan. Five moves, one at a time, and each one feeds the next.
By the end, you'll have the whole machine.
Quick note. I'm a stick figure, not your financial advisor. This is education, not advice.
Move one. Pay yourself first.
Here's how most people do it. Paycheck comes in. You pay rent, food, fun, and whatever is left at the end, you save.
Here's the thing. There is never anything left.
So flip the order. The day your pay arrives, a fixed slice goes straight to savings, before you touch a cent.
Then you live on the rest.
This works because of a weird trick of the brain. Money you never see, you don't miss. Put your savings in a separate account, one that doesn't show up every time you open your spending app.
It doesn't have to be big. Start with a slice that doesn't hurt, and nudge it up every time you get a raise.
And automate it. Set up an automatic transfer, so willpower never gets a vote.
Boring. And that's the point.
Move two. Kill high-interest debt.
Saving money while you carry credit card debt is like filling a bucket with a hole in the bottom.
Card interest compounds against you. For example, three thousand dollars at twenty-two percent a year costs you over seven hundred dollars in interest in a single year, if you don't pay it down.
That's money you worked for, buying absolutely nothing.
So, list your debts. Pay the minimum on all of them, and throw every spare dollar at the one with the highest interest rate.
When it's gone, roll that payment into the next one. It speeds up, like a snowball.
Some people prefer to clear the smallest balance first, for the quick win. That's fine too. The best plan is the one you'll actually stick with.
And while you're digging out, stop adding new debt. You can't empty a bath with the tap still running.
And keep a small emergency fund, so one flat tire doesn't put you right back on the card.
Move three. Invest early, and let time do the heavy lifting.
Compounding means your money earns money, and then that money earns money too.
Watch. This is me. I put two hundred dollars a month into a low-cost index fund, starting at twenty-five.
This is Larry. Larry does the exact same thing, but he waits until he's thirty-five.
To keep the math simple, let's assume seven percent a year on average. That's an assumption, not a promise. Real markets jump around.
At sixty-five, Larry has put in seventy-two thousand dollars, and ends up with about two hundred and forty thousand.
I put in ninety-six thousand. Only twenty-four thousand more. And I end up with about five hundred and twenty-five thousand.
Same habit. Ten extra years. More than double the money. The difference wasn't talent. It was time.
And an index fund just means you own a tiny slice of hundreds of companies at once, so you're not betting everything on one.
And if your job offers a retirement plan with an employer match, take the full match first. It's the closest thing to free money you'll ever be offered.
Keep the fees low, keep adding, and don't panic sell when it drops. It will drop. Stay on the hill.
Move four. Grow your income, then guard it.
Cutting costs has a floor. You can only skip so many coffees. But earning has no ceiling.
The best investment is usually you. A skill that's in demand. Getting really good at something people pay for.
It doesn't take a degree. Ten minutes a day, every day, adds up to more than sixty hours of practice in a year.
Then use it. Ask for the raise, with proof. Switch jobs if yours won't pay what you're worth. Or start something on the side.
But here's the trap. When income goes up, spending sneaks up right behind it.
So when you get a raise, send at least half of it straight to move one and move three. Live a little better, not a lot better.
Move five. Own things that earn while you sleep.
There are two kinds of stuff. Things that take money out of your pocket, and things that put money into it.
A new car loses value as soon as you drive it home. Shares in companies, a small business, things you create that keep selling. Those can pay you again and again.
Your job trades hours for money, and you only have so many hours.
Owning things breaks that link. That's how wealth stops depending on how hard you work today.
Start small. Ownership can be one share, or one thing you built on a weekend.
And remember, the skills you built in move four are an asset too. Nobody can repossess what you know.
So that's the machine.
Pay yourself first, so money exists.
Kill the debt, so nothing leaks.
Invest it, so it grows.
Grow your income, so there's more to feed in.
And own things that earn, so it keeps going without you.
Notice what's missing. No lottery. No hot tip. No coin your cousin swears is going to the moon.
If anything promises you fast and guaranteed, run.
Getting rich is mostly boring stuff, done for a long time. And the earlier you start, the less boring stuff you need.

scenes.chapter: What a real month looks like

lines.text: So what does this look like in a real month? Let's walk through one payday.
Day one. Pay lands. The automatic transfer moves your slice to savings, before you even wake up.
Minimum payments go out on every debt, and the extra goes to the most expensive one.
Another slice goes into your index fund. Same amount, every month, no matter what the news says.
And what's left is yours. Rent, food, fun. No guilt, because the important stuff already happened.
Then you do it again next month. And the month after that. That's the whole trick.
So here's your one job. Tonight, set up one automatic transfer. Any amount. That's move one, and the machine starts turning.
I'll see you in the next one.

me-vs-larry.text: You and Larry both save $200 a month. He starts 10 years later. Why does he end up with less than half?

hole-in-the-bucket.text: $3,000 on a card at 22% can cost you over $700 in one year. That's why your savings never grow.

flip-the-order.text: You save what's left at the end of the month? Stop. That's why there's never anything left.

no-ceiling.text: You can only cut so many coffees before you hit the floor. Earning has no ceiling, but almost nobody guards it.

the-money-machine.text: Stop waiting for a raise to get rich. 5 gears, a normal salary, and almost nobody builds all 5.
